 OpenAI CEO Sam Altman outlines three possible approaches to AI safety
 OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are pursuing a joint US AI safety initiative, while disagreements over model testing and regulatory oversight continue to complicate efforts to establish common safeguards. 
 By   Storyboard18 |  October 23, 2026, 10:16:02 IST Choose Storyboard18 on Follow Share Sam Altman weighs three AI safety models as OpenAI faces one-year deadline
 ADVERTISEMENT
 OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has outlined three possible approaches to managing the risks of advanced artificial intelligence, telling employees that the company must decide which path to support within a year, according to a report by The Information . 
 The discussion comes as the Donald Trump administration works on its first framework to oversee developers of superintelligent AI. The proposals include international regulation, a shared AI research organisation and a scenario in which one developer gains control over rivals' access to computing resources. 
 Three approaches to AI safety 
 The first proposal involves an international body modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which would monitor AI development and enforce safety standards. Altman appeared to favour this option, according to The Information .

In a proposal that year, Altman, president Greg Brockman and then-chief scientist Ilya Sutskever suggested that it could inspect AI systems, require audits and track computing and energy use. 
 The second option, called the “Demis plan” by Altman, draws on an idea associated with Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis . It envisages a CERN-like organisation through which major AI companies would provide models to partner countries. 
 The third, known as the “Eliezer plan”, is named after AI safety researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky. It describes a scenario in which a developer achieves self-improving AI and uses its economic power to restrict competitors' access to computing chips. 
 Altman reportedly opposed this outcome and included it only for completeness. Some OpenAI employees viewed the remark as a possible dig at Anthropic, given Yudkowsky's links to the company, The Information reported. 
 AI safety efforts gather pace 
 The discussion follows security incidents involving AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta. OpenAI and Anthropic are also moving towards public listings, intensifying competitive pressures. 
 OpenAI , Google and Anthropic are working on a US-based group called the Standards Authority for Frontier AI, which they aim to launch by early 2027. The companies, however, differ on how new models should be tested. 
 Anthropic has separately proposed draft legislation that would allow the US Commerce Department to halt models capable of causing large-scale harm. 
 Under the US government's current voluntary framework, developers are asked to provide access to certain AI models up to 30 days before release. On September 29, executives from Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, Nvidia and xAI signed a voluntary accord that Trump described as “morally binding”, although it carries no legal liability. 
 Altman's reported one-year timeline puts pressure on OpenAI to identify its preferred approach as the industry continues to pursue advances in AI while debating how to manage the associated risks.
